Sorry for conflicting instructions :/ As @aaronfranke, we're going to enforce brackets around single line `if`/`else` blocks in 4.0, but this will be done all at once using a dedicated tool.

Until then, it's better to just use such brackets around new code, but not to modify existing code to follow that convention unless it's only a few lines or directly around the code being changed. So the code style fixes you made now make it somewhat harder to see what are the actual logic changes in this relatively sensitive code (`base_button.cpp` is the base for all button nodes, so any wrong change here will impact all Godot GUIs).

So while it's not bad per se now, I would prefer it if the PR did not change the style of code which does not have logic changes, so that we can easily review each changed line.

You'd also have to squash the commits together so that the PR contains only one commit (currently it has two). See [PR workflow](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/community/contributing/pr_workflow.html#mastering-the-pr-workflow-the-rebase) for details.
About the commit message, your second commit is indeed more verbose than the first one, but I'd argue it's a bit too verbose now. It's not a big deal either, and figuring out how to write "good" commit logs is a matter of experience so don't worry about it.

I'd suggest something like this for the final commit:
```
Allow custom color for hover_pressed on CheckButton and CheckBox

Fixes #34727.
```

As outlined in [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#format-your-commit-logs-with-readability-in-mind), the commit message is structured in two sections: the title, which should be a short, single line, and then the body of the message which can be as long as necessary to provide more details. Only the title will appear in `git shortlog`, changelogs or when reviewing commits on GitHub, unless you click the `...` button for details. Official recommendation is to keep the title below 50 chars, but in my experience that's very difficult to achieve while keeping things readable, so it's OK to go slightly over it as done in my example (but I still reduced "Makes it possible to have" to "Allow" to be more concise).

I know it's a lot of info and changes requested, so it may feel overwhelming. But don't worry, we're also here to help you hone your FOSS contribution skills both for Godot and other future projects you make work on :)

> Though the agents are a bit jittery and sometimes become sluggish, is this expected, and to be resolved by the end implementation of the game?

Yes this is expected. You have to set the agent properties (like `Time Horizon`, `Max Speed`) properly so the Agent can decide to react earlier or later to an obstacle.

This is a feature. The `Agent` doesn't control the `start` nor the `end` of the path resolution, but this is up to the developer decide how to use it. In my case, I've decided to run the path resolution endless so even if the character reached the final destination it can still fight to be more near possible to the end.

I have updated the PR with some deferring mechanics inspired by the existing codebase:
```cpp
t->call_deferred("emit_signal", "completed", t->ret);
```
as in here for instance:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/a1ab8f889032fbf779b5bd5a08e6bae9e15aafce/editor/editor_resource_preview.cpp#L453-L455

Doing so allows to use yiedling combined with threads:

```gdscript
thread.start(self, "_image_process", "res://mona.png")
var result = yield(thread, "completed") # returns whatever the thread was supposed to return
$sprite.texture = thread.wait_to_finish() # returns the result too, but also finalizes the thread
```

And the user doesn't have to worry about connecting the signal with `CONNECT_DEFERRED`):
```gdscript
thread.connect("completed", self, "_on_thread_completed") # that's it
```

I'm not sure how well this would actually work with mutexes and stuff, but for simple cases works flawlessly with the demo I linked.

I think this is a misunderstanding of how signals work, so implementing something like what you want to implement is effectively not even possible.

body:
Tested with my PS3 controller reported by the OS as:
```
MY-POWER CO.,LTD. USB Joystick
030000008f0e00000300000010010000
```

The mappings were correct but wrongly reported as `GreenAsia Inc. USB Joystick ` (note trailing whitespace) which is a mapping from `gamecontrollerdb_204.txt` (there's an equivalent in `gamecontrollerdb_205.txt` with no trailing whitespace).
In `gamecontrollerdb.txt`, this device is reported as "PS3 Controller", and this is what https://github.com/godotengine/godot-demo-projects/tree/master/misc/joypads now properly reports.

In my case the issue was only with the name (mappings are the same), but for users where there might be a wrong/outdated mapping in `_204` or `_205` that would override a better mapping of the `gamecontrollerdb.txt`, this could explain badly functioning controllers.

We may want to consider dropping the `_204` and `_205` variants altogether, I'm not sure they're needed. We'd have to check if any of their GUID are actually missing from `gamecontrollerdb.txt`.

body:
@AndreaCatania, please explain what problem this change is solving, because, from what I can see, this will change the behaviour of how `stop_on_slope` works.

Currently, if the user wants the `KinematicBody` to not slide down a slope, the user calls `move_and_slide()` or `move_and_slide_with_snap()` and specifies the direction of the `floor normal` (normally up) and sets `stop_on_slope` to true. The user can also specify the `floor_max_angle` which defaults to 45°, which puts a limit on the angle considered a floor and hence the limit for the `stop_on_slope`. If the current `linear_velocity` passed is in the opposite direction to the `floor_normal` (i.e. normally directly down), the `KinematicBody` will not slide and the velocity returned will be zero. This zero velocity is normally feedback as the `linear_velocity` to the next call to `move_and_slide()` or `move_and_slide_with_snap()`, so the body stops.

If the current velocity is not in the opposite direction to the `floor_normal` (i.e. not just "falling" but moving) the body will slide and the velocity returned will be the updated velocity perpendicular to the collision normal.

I could be wrong, because I haven't tested it, but it looks like, this change will consider any movement up to the `floor_max_angle` (i.e. if it's on a floor) will now be stopped and a zero velocity returned if `stop_on_slope` is true. This would effectively be similar behaviour to `move_and_collide` (although sliding would still occur on walls and ceilings).

body:
> Can you please explain what "behaviour change" mean for you? because I don't really see your point.

By behaviour change, I mean a change from the [documented behaviour](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.1/classes/class_kinematicbody.html#class-kinematicbody-method-move-and-slide) of the function.

Unfortunately, the current documented behaviour of the `stop_on_slope` parameter is open to interpretation: "If `stop_on_slope` is `true`, body will not slide on slopes if you include gravity in `linear_velocity`."

Assuming that "include gravity" means have a negative `y` component in `linear_velocity` when the `floor_normal` equals `Vector.UP`, taken literally, this definition would result in the `KinematicBody` stopping on all surfaces that are considered slopes i.e. be the same as `move_and_collide()`. This is probably not the intended behaviour. The original PR (with [`f7d98c1`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/f7d98c1de2a365d6ebc976f81191b8e7f7c116c9)) would have resulted in this behaviour.

Instead, the current interpretation (assuming `floor_normal` equals `Vector.UP`) checks if the `linear_velocity` only has a negative `y` component, or more generally, if the `linear_velocity` and `floor_normal` vectors passed by the user are in opposite directions. It achieves this by checking if the combination of the normal (or direction) of the`linear_velocity` and `floor_normal` vectors passed by the user, has a length of less than a small value:
``` (body_velocity_normal + p_up_direction).length() < 0.01 ```
where `body_velocity_normal` equals `linear_velocity.normalized()` and `p_up_direction` equals `floor_normal`.

The result is, if `floor_normal` equals `Vector.UP`, the `linear_velocity` must have a negative `y` component and a `x` value (or `sqrt(x² + z²)` in the 3D case) of less than 0.01 times the length of the `y` component, which, to all intents and purposes requires the `x` and `z` components to be zero.

> The velocity is supposed to be always parallel to the ground. So the 10 deg mean that the player can climb up to 80 degrees slopes. It's quite unrealistic that someone want to climb such angles so it's not a number that fits only my use cases.

This PR currently (with  bd48323) proposes changing the above check to:
``` (body_velocity_normal.dot(p_up_direction) < COS_DOWN_DIRECTION_THRESHOLD ```
where COS_DOWN_DIRECTION_THRESHOLD is set to -0.98480774002 derived from -cos(10°). The dot product of two vectors **a** and **b** is [defined](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_product) geometrically as ||**a**|| ||**b**|| cos(_θ_), where _θ_ is the angle between the two vectors and the magnitude of a vector **a** is denoted ||**a**||. Since both vectors (assuming `floor_normal` is Vector.UP) have a magnitude of 1, this simply checks that the angle between the two vectors is between 170° and 190° (-cos(10°) = cos(170°) = cos(190°)) i.e. roughly pointing in opposite directions. This effectively increases the tolerance of the size of the `x` value (or `sqrt(x² + z²)` in the 3D case) to less than approximately 0.17 times the `y` component.

> > In short, I don't think changing Godot's behaviour to fix for a specific use-case is the solution.

>Well, this is not at all what it's happening here

Since `move_and_slide()` uses
``` linear_velocity - floor_normal * linear_velocity.dot(floor_normal) ```
to calculate the returned velocity, the `x` component (or `sqrt(x² + z²)` in the 3D case) returned will be tan(_α_) times the size of the `y` component, where _α_ is the angle of the slope. For slope angles below the 10° currently defined by this PR, the `x` component (or `sqrt(x² + z²)` in the 3D case) will be less than the required 0.17 times the `y` component, for slope angles above 10°, the user's controller will still need to reduce this `x` value (or `sqrt(x² + z²)` in the 3D case) to less than 0.17 times the `y` component to stop the `KinematicBody` from sliding.

Conversely, with this PR, other controllers, which currently clamp the `x` (and `z` components) to zero when required, will now stick on flat surfaces for velocities with an `x` value (or `sqrt(x² + z²)` in the 3D case) of less than 0.17 times the `y`component instead being able to smoothly accelerate by slowly increasing the `x` component.


In short this PR provides a hard-coded snapping function, which may not be sufficient for some users' controllers and may be undesired for other users' controllers.

I agree that the `stop_on_slope` doesn't work as desired, but I don't agree that this PR is the solution. It will fix specific use cases, but not all, and it will create new issues. The API needs to be fixed, but, as I stated previously, the interface and its desired behaviour should be agreed first.

body: @madmiraal Considering this check`(body_velocity_normal + p_up_direction).length() < 0.01` do we agree that `0.01` is not an angle but rather a meaningless distance and there are more meaningful way to check the velocity direction in respect to the `up_direction` that can improve future maintanance?
author: AndreaCatania

body:
> @madmiraal Considering this check `(body_velocity_normal + p_up_direction).length() < 0.01` do we agree that `0.01` is not an angle but rather a meaningless distance and there are more meaningful way to check the velocity direction in respect to the `up_direction` that can improve future maintanance?

`0.01` is simply a small value to allow for the numerical imprecision of floats. It could probably have been set to `UNIT_EPSILON`.

`(body_velocity_normal + p_up_direction).length() < 0.01` checks to see whether the direction of the `linear_velocity` vector and the `up_direction` vector (both passed by the user) are in opposite directions. Note: It assumes the users passes a normalised vector as the `up_direction` parameter.

If the user passes `Vector.UP` as the `up_direction` parameter, this provides a simple check that the `y` component of `linear_velocity` is negative and the `x` and `z` components are zero, while allowing for scenarios when the user chooses another direction for up.

In turn, it provides a simple way for the user to stop the `KinematicBody` from sliding when using `move_and_slide()` or `move_and_slide_with_snap()` and `stop_on_slide` is set to `true`: Simply make the `x` and `z` components zero.

The problem arises when the user uses a controller that doesn't set the 'x' and 'z' components to zero when there is no input. Rather the 'x' and 'z' components are moved incrementally towards zero. This is done to provide a smooth deceleration. However, this approach fails when combining it with `move_and_slide()` or `move_and_slide_with_snap()` and the increment towards zero is less than the change generated by the slide. This problem is difficult for the user to solve, because the change generated by the slide is dependent on the steepness of the slope, and many are simply copying another controller and expecting it to work in all scenarios.

Therefore, this is not a problem with the slide functionality of the `move_and_slide()` and `move_and_slide_with_snap()` functions. They are doing what they are supposed to. The problem is the user doesn't understand why on some slopes their character slides down.

The solution is to ensure that the `x` and `z` components are snapped to zero when required, but the user should specify when this is required. This allows the user to fine-tune it to her requirements. The `move_and_slide()` and `move_and_slide_with_snap()` functions should not be specifying when this is required or even that it is required.

Remember, the `move_and_slide()` and `move_and_slide_with_snap()` functions are convenience functions. The user doesn't need to use them. All the functionality can be done by the user using `move_and_collide()` and updating their character's velocity using the [`KinematicCollision`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.1/classes/class_kinematiccollision.html) or [`KinematicCollision2D`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.1/classes/class_kinematiccollision2d.html) object returned. This is after all what `move_and_slide()` is doing, and what `move_and_slide_with_snap()` is doing by calling `move_and_slide()`.

The reason they are provided as convenience functions is that they are both common requirements, and, move importantly, it is difficult to calculate the updated velocity vector from the collision normal to generate a slide. `linear_velocity - floor_normal * linear_velocity.dot(floor_normal)` is not intuitive, but it works and it also automatically reduces the velocity proportional to the steepness of the slope albeit not in a correct physics way.

In short, I don't agree that `0.01` is "a meaningless distance" or that there is a need for a "more meaningful way to check the velocity direction". I do agree there is a need to update the existing code to "improve future _maintenance_".

body:
It sounds like you're looking for the collision normal: the normal at the point of collision of the surface of the body the `KinematicBody` is colliding with. This is already stored in the `normal` property of the [`KinematicCollision`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.1/classes/class_kinematiccollision.html) object.

Unlike `move_and_collide()`, the `move_and_slide()` and `move_and_slide_with_snap()` functions can result in up to a `max_slides` number of collisions. Therefore, the `KinematicCollision` objects are not returned, and they need to be retrieved separately using [`get_slide_collision()`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.1/classes/class_kinematicbody.html#class-kinematicbody-method-get-slide-collision).

body:
> This function is used to retrieve with only one function call the floor normal of the surface. What's wrong with that?

I'm not saying it's wrong. I was asking why it is needed. What was wrong with the previous way?:
```
if get_slide_count() > 0 && is_on_floor():
	floor_normal = get_slide_collision(get_slide_count() - 1).normal
```
The new `get_floor_normal()` function will return a value even if there was no collision and, if there was a collision, even if the collision was not with a user defined floor. The previous way at least required the user to perform the necessary checks before assuming there was a normal and, if there was, that it was a floor.

Regardless of whether or not we needed to help the user by simplifying the above, there is still the issue that if the `KinematicBody` does not collide with a user defined floor, the new function will return the user defined `p_up_direction`:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/dbbfade584ed5f1ecedd8ce78552e90df66a538d/scene/2d/physics_body_2d.cpp#L1237-L1238
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/dbbfade584ed5f1ecedd8ce78552e90df66a538d/scene/3d/physics_body.cpp#L1162-L1163

Rather, this should probably be a zero vector; as is done with `floor_velocity`.

Regarding changing `p_floor_direction` to `p_up_direction`. If this is for the user's benefit, then all the four `move_and_slide*()` functions' bindings should have been changed too. Currently only one has been changed.

Finally, the documentation should be updated. The `get_floor_normal()` functions should be consistent with the `get_floor_velocity()` functions and explain when they are valid. Similarly, the `move_and_slide*()` functions should be updated to use the `up_direction` value.

I'll submit a PR to fix these three things.

body:
> I'm not very familiar with godot source code, but as far as I understand this keeps only GDScript object with a global class name loaded
> can you explain what you mean by "everything with a class_name"?

It's what you just said. When you use `class_name` in the script, you're adding it to the global scope (so it will be a "GDScript object with a global class name"). Many people like to give name to all their scripts, so this will keep all scripts loaded. And if those scripts use `preload`, this will also keep those resources alive for the whole application. As you did here, if you never load them it'll be fine, but if you load them once they'll never be unloaded, which isn't desirable.

And this also won't solve the cases when you *don't* have a `class_name` and is using `preload` instead.

> If you have any other idea how to solve it I would be glad to give it a try.

I don't really have one. But I don't like adding this even as workaround, since it's essentially introducing a memory leak for users' projects, even for those who didn't bump into the issue.

body: ``COLOR`` is set in the vertex function based on the underlying primitive (which can be a mesh). It can be modified in the vertex function, and then it is passed into the fragment. With this PR, the information coming in from the primitive will be disregarded. That will break a lot of users scripts and make it impossible to utilize per-vertex colors (that are passed in from CPU). Additionally, many users user ``COLOR`` as a generic way to get four per-vertex floats of custom data into the shader.

author: Chaosus

body:
I don't think #25009 is even a bug. Users are expecting a texture lookup to occur for them, but that isn't what the ``COLOR`` variable is for. 

I think you have done the best implementation possible, but I think it still creates confusing behaviour. 

The issue is, if we make it so that the texture lookup is done when users only try to alter a single channel e.g. ``COLOR.a = 0.5``, then they are always going to expect that ``COLOR`` contains the value of the texture lookup. So if they change their code to ``COLOR.rgba = vec4(0.5)`` suddenly the texture will disappear and be replaced by a grey box.

The only consistent behaviour is to make ``COLOR`` always be the color from the vertex function. For 4.0 we can discuss changing the API so that we have ``COLOR`` and ``MODULATE_COLOR`` or something to avoid this confusion.

body:
### Updates (last 8 commits):
* Add FastNoiseSIMD
* Hardware specific compiler flags in scons
* Many other tweaks

FastNoiseSIMD is has nearly all the features of FastNoise, except these:
1. Lookups of singular values (e.g. f = get_noise_3d(x,y,z) ) doesn't exist natively. All lookups are done in sets. I've added singular lookup functions, however they are 3x slower than the regular FastNoise
1. No 4D simplex (disabled anyway) or whitenoise. 
1. Recursive cellular lookups aren't as featureful. On FN, you get a whole secondary FN object and can control all settings. On SIMD, you can only specify the secondary type and a few other things. So there's no way to achieve this look directly in SIMD:
![image](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/c877b3cb4240ef7641f141acc5c7f0047cb32bf6/68747470733a2f2f7062732e7477696d672e636f6d2f6d656469612f454f52624f55565641414543595a593f666f726d61743d6a7067266e616d653d6c61726765)

### Benchmarks
I chose Perlin Fractal as the default values look most like OpenSimplexNoise. Metrics are ms needed to generate and normalize a 2D image within Godot. SIMD are using AVX2 on a Core i7-8570H.

|   | 1k | 2k | 4k |
---|---|---|---
OpenSimplexNoise | 107 | 435 | 1730 |
FN Perlin Fractal | 104 | 400 | 1600 |
SIMD Perlin Fractal (singular) | 304 | 1210 | 4800 | 
SIMD Perlin Fractal | 28 | 107 | 430 | 
---|---|---|---
FN Value | 74 | 294 | 
SIMD Value | 13 | 44 |
---|---|---|---
FN Heavily tweaked Cellular |  | 2284 |
SIMD Heavily tweaked Cellular |  | 229 |

FastNoiseSIMD generating basic 2D textures is 4-6x faster than FastNoise, and gets even faster as the algorithms gets more complex, even into 3D. Generating large blocks of noise can be split up into multiple threads becoming *another* 3-7x faster or (up to 40x faster than FastNoise)! [pyFastNoiseSIMD benchmarks](https://github.com/robbmcleod/pyfastnoisesimd)

On #22337 @Calinou asked if the performance as good on hardware that can't take advantage of it. All new intel 64-bit processors have SSE2 built in, so I can't turn it off, but I can compare regular, SSE2 and AVX2. I'd guess the SIMD sets w/o SIMD is as good regular FN. Maybe better because the algorithm is working in one set, rather than being called for every individual pixel/voxel. This is generating a 1k image using the author's [demo app](https://github.com/Auburns/FastNoiseSIMD/releases/tag/0.7):

|   | FN | SIMD SSE2 | SIMD AVX2 
---|---|---|---
Value | 66| 23 | 6 
Perlin Fractal | 108 | 94 | 43
Cellular Noise Lookup to Simplex | 96 | 117 | 61
Cellular Distance2 Sub | 209 | 75 | 30 



### Questions

#### 1. Both classes or combined or...?
~~SIMD singular lookups are a waste of time. We could:~~
~~* Keep both classes and provide only sets in SIMD and only singular in FN.~~
~~* I could maybe combine them into one class. The features are almost the same, but there are some differences. That means some combination of features won't return anything, and definitely the noise pattern from the singular version will not match the set version. Least preferred option.~~
~~* SIMD could be considered too fringe use and be a separate module not in core. But the use case is definitely needed for @Zylann and me in Voxel Tools as OSN is a bottleneck.~~
Edit: SIMD and FN return different noise values. SIMD needs the singular values though slow. The question is still open as to whether both libraries are included or only one.

#### 2. Memory, Pointers, & References
FastNoiseSIMD GetNoiseSet() returns a pointer to a float array allocated with _aligned_malloc, posix_memalign, (or new if no SIMD avail). 

~~* Is there a way to add this memory into a Ref or some other mechanism so Godot can manage it?~~

* I wrote in some basic memory management ([here](https://github.com/tinmanjuggernaut/godot/blob/dc11b20990d7f5ea7446f7cf90d13b4c1503f4fc/modules/noise/fast_noise_simd.cpp#L63) and [here](https://github.com/tinmanjuggernaut/godot/blob/dc11b20990d7f5ea7446f7cf90d13b4c1503f4fc/modules/noise/fast_noise_simd.cpp#L164)) that keeps a linked list of all sets that have been allocated and deletes them upon request or upon the destructor (FastNoiseSIMD.cpp). Is this sufficient?

~~* Am I correct in thinking that there is no way to pass by reference in GDScript? I was thinking I could leave the function returning float* for C++ use. Then for GDSCript provide a separate function that returns a PoolRealArray and copy all of the elements into it. Seems kinda clunky.~~

~~* Is there a way to override functions so I can do the above and use the same names for C++ and GDScript? The macros complain about the same names. Is the convention to use _function for public C++ use?~~

#### 3. Namespace
* How do I properly namespace `FastNoiseSIMD`? FN had its own namespace, so a simple `typedef fastnoise::FastNoise _FastNoise;` allowed us to use `FastNoise`. SIMD has an internal namespace, but it's public class does not. When trying to add a namespace in the same way as FN I ran into too many name scope issues from the internal class, so I just ended up renaming the public class. Is there a better way?


~~#### 4. Crashes~~
~~So far what I've been doing has been stable aside from obvious bugs. But only just today, and only on occasion, when changing noise values, Godot has hung with this repeating in the console. I don't think I'm causing this. Anyone know what this could be?~~
```
ERROR: RichTextLabel::_process_line: Index line=0 out of size (l.offset_caches.size()=0)
   At: scene\gui\rich_text_label.cpp:170
```
Edit: this hasn't repeated

FastNoiseSIMD compiles fine with windows/msvc or linux/gcc. However, it won't compile with mingw-w64 which is used in the official dockers to cross-compile for windows from Linux. 

The issue is that it won't properly preprocess a statement like this and produces thousands of errors.
```
FastNoiseSIMD_internal.cpp:43:22: error: expected initializer before 'L3_FUNC_Lerp'
 #define L_VAR2(x, l) L##l##_##x
                      ^
FastNoiseSIMD_internal.cpp:44:21: note: in expansion of macro 'L_VAR2'
 #define L_VAR(x, l) L_VAR2(x, l)
                     ^~~~~~
FastNoiseSIMD_internal.cpp:45:16: note: in expansion of macro 'L_VAR'
 #define VAR(x) L_VAR(x, SIMD_LEVEL)
                ^~~~~
FastNoiseSIMD_internal.cpp:46:17: note: in expansion of macro 'VAR'
 #define FUNC(x) VAR(FUNC_##x)
                 ^~~
FastNoiseSIMD_internal.cpp:682:25: note: in expansion of macro 'FUNC'
 static SIMDf VECTORCALL FUNC(Lerp)(SIMDf a, SIMDf b, SIMDf t)
                         ^~~~
```

I've been able to work around that by having gcc/linux preprocess it, then passing that to mingw, but there are other compiling issues I haven't been able to resolve. 

However, even if I were to nail those down, the other problem is that mingw-w64 doesn't support AVX byte alignment and allegedly will crash even if it does compile. This issue has persisted for years. Apparently cygwin/gcc, llvm, linux/gcc, and msvc don't share this issue.

So, my thinking is that this PR will be limited to just FastNoise and Noise, and I can package up my FastNoiseSIMD work as a separate module so people can build it themselves. At least until Godot moves off of mingw for official builds, or mingw fixes the issue; though both are unlikely.

Unless there are other suggestions?

I also looked at how cellular noise is implemented and tbh I think it might have a specialization too (without fractal), because it can output multiple informations at once (cell values and cell distances). I'm using it for a different purpose so I didn't implement stuff like seamless textures, but should be easy to add from how this PR did.

What motivated me was the speed of 3D OpenSimplex2 noise, which is twice as fast compared to Godot's current version. And of course the other noise types which are even faster and often good enough.

var x = "test"

(test: 5)

Some info about audio server
* Audio threads must _never_ do anything that risks a kernel preemption, which includes system calls.
* Memory allocation causes system calls, and signal emission in some cases may do it
* Emitting signals from anything other than the main thread is unsafe, because connecting/disconnecting/emitting is not.
* There are better ways to hook to capture or play audio, just create your own audio effect and put it in a bus.

Closing for a better implementation.

> Godot has a RingBuffer class you can check as reference, you need two of those

> Your AudioEffect is fed audio and expects you to feed audio back in a single callback

> The audio you are fed is pushed to the ringbuffer, and you pull from the second ringbuffer for audio to push

> https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/a7f49ac9a107820a62677ee3fb49d38982a25165/core/ring_buffer.h

> In another thread, which is updated periodically, you fill packets by reading from the first ringbuffer and send them, and you decompress packets you get and feed them to the second ringbuffer

> [reduz] that said, I feel that is not a great approach for voip, since you need to account for many different situations like delays and running out of packets. I am sure there are better implementations out there

> [reduz] also you need to account for packets arriving out of order and that kind of stuff
